plain_english: Every habit and skill gets stronger when you practice it. Walking gets easier by walking. Running gets easier by running. Want to be a good reader? Read. Want to be a writer? Write. But if you don't read for thirty days straight and do other things instead, you'll see what happens. Same thing if you lie in bed for ten days, then get up and try to take a long walk. Your legs will be weak. So here's the rule: if you want to build a habit, do it. If you don't want a habit, don't do it. Train yourself to do something else instead.
original_excerpt: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running. If you would be a good reader, read; if a writer, write. But when you shall not have read for thirty days in succession, but have done something else, you will know the consequence. In the same way, if you shall have lain down ten days, get up and attempt to make a long walk, and you will see how your legs are weakened. Generally then if you would make anything a habit, do it; if you would not make it a habit, do not do it, but accustom yourself to do something else in place of it.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances

plain_english: This is how mental diseases grow, according to philosophers. Say you want money. If you use reason to see that this desire is harmful, you can stop it. Your mind returns to its natural, healthy state. But if you don't treat the problem, things get worse. The next time something triggers that desire, it flares up faster and stronger than before. Keep letting this happen, and the desire hardens into a permanent condition. The mental disease takes hold completely. It's like physical fever. Someone who recovers from fever isn't the same as someone who was never sick — unless they're completely cured. Mental diseases work the same way. They leave traces and tender spots in your soul. If you don't heal them completely, the next time you get hit in those same spots, you won't just get blisters. You'll get open wounds.
original_excerpt: In this manner certainly, as philosophers say, also diseases of the mind grow up. For when you have once desired money, if reason be applied to lead to a perception of the evil, the desire is stopped, and the ruling faculty of our mind is restored to the original authority. But if you apply no means of cure, it no longer returns to the same state, but being again excited by the corresponding appearance, it is inflamed to desire quicker than before: and when this takes place continually, it is henceforth hardened (made callous), and the disease of the mind confirms the love of money. For he who has had a fever, and has been relieved from it, is not in the same state that he was before, unless he has been completely cured. Something of the kind happens also in diseases of the soul. Certain traces and blisters are left in it, and unless a man shall completely efface them, when he is again lashed on the same places, the lash will produce not blisters (weals) but sores.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances

plain_english: If you don't want to be an angry person, don't feed the habit. Don't give it anything that will make it stronger. Start by staying quiet and counting the days you didn't get angry. I used to get mad every day. Then it was every other day. Then every third day, then every fourth. If you go thirty days without anger, make an offering to God. The habit gets weaker at first, then it's completely destroyed. "I haven't been upset today, or yesterday, or for two or three months now. But I was careful when things happened that could set me off." Trust me — you're on the right track.
original_excerpt: If then you wish not to be of an angry temper, do not feed the habit: throw nothing on it which will increase it: at first keep quiet, and count the days on which you have not been angry. I used to be in passion every day; now every second day; then every third, then every fourth. But if you have intermitted thirty days, make a sacrifice to God. For the habit at first begins to be weakened, and then is completely destroyed. "I have not been vexed to-day, nor the day after, nor yet on any succeeding day during two or three months; but I took care when some exciting things happened." Be assured that you are in a good way.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances

plain_english: How do you do this? Start wanting to approve of yourself. Want to appear beautiful to God. Desire to be pure with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such temptation visits you, Plato says: Go through purification rituals. Go as a beggar to the temples of the gods who turn away evil. It's even enough if you spend time with noble and just people. Compare yourself with them, whether you find someone living or dead.
original_excerpt: How then shall this be done? Be willing at length to be approved by yourself, be willing to appear beautiful to God, desire to be in purity with your own pure self and with God. Then when any such appearance visits you, Plato says, Have recourse to expiations, go a suppliant to the temples of the averting deities. It is even sufficient if you resort to the society of noble and just men, and compare yourself with them, whether you find one who is living or dead.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances

plain_english: First, don't let your immediate reactions sweep you away. When something appears in your mind, say, "Wait a minute. Let me see what you really are. Let me test you." Don't let that first impression take over and paint vivid pictures of what might happen next. If you do, it will drag you wherever it wants. Instead, bring in a better, nobler thought to fight against it. Push out the ugly thought. If you practice this regularly, you'll see what real strength and power you have. But right now, you're just talking about it and nothing more.
original_excerpt: But in the first place, be not hurried away by the rapidity of the appearance, but say, Appearances, wait for me a little; let me see who you are, and what you are about; let me put you to the test. And then do not allow the appearance to lead you on and draw lively pictures of the things which will follow; for if you do, it will carry you off wherever it pleases. But rather bring in to oppose it some other beautiful and noble appearance, and cast out this base appearance. And if you are accustomed to be exercised in this way, you will see what shoulders, what sinews, what strength you have. But now it is only trifling words, and nothing more.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances

plain_english: This is what a true athlete looks like — someone who trains against these mental impressions. Stop right there, you fool. Don't let yourself get swept away. This is a huge fight. The work is sacred. You're fighting for control, for freedom, for happiness, for peace of mind. Remember God. Call on him to help and protect you, like sailors call on their gods during a storm. What storm is worse than the one that comes from violent impressions that drive away your reason? The storm itself — what is it but an impression? Take away your fear of death. Let there be as much thunder and lightning as you want. You'll see how calm and peaceful your mind can be. But if you lose once and say "I'll win next time," then say the same thing again, you can be sure you'll end up so miserable and weak that you won't even know you're doing wrong anymore. You'll start making excuses for your bad behavior. Then you'll prove Hesiod right: "The person who keeps putting things off struggles with constant troubles."
original_excerpt: This is the true athlete, the man who exercises himself against such appearances. Stay, wretch, do not be carried away. Great is the combat, divine is the work; it is for kingship, for freedom, for happiness, for freedom from perturbation. Remember God; call on him as a helper and protector, as men at sea call on the Dioscuri in a storm. For what is a greater storm than that which comes from appearances which are violent and drive away the reason? For the storm itself, what else is it but an appearance? For take away the fear of death, and suppose as many thunders and lightnings as you please, and you will know what calm and serenity there is in the ruling faculty. But if you have once been defeated and say that you will conquer hereafter, and then say the same again, be assured that you will at last be in so wretched a condition and so weak that you will not even know afterwards that you are doing wrong, but you will even begin to make apologies (defences) for your wrong-doing, and then you will confirm the saying of Hesiod to be true, With constant ills the dilatory strives.
source_reference: Discourses, How We Should Struggle Against Appearances
